clock.title: The Earth's motions on one clock, at their true speeds
clock.mini: One hand for the Earth's rotation, one for its orbit, two for the slow swing of its axis and of its orbit, one for the Sun around the Galaxy: each at its true angle now, none sped up.
clock.text: Each hand turns at the true rate of one of the Earth's motions, on the clock of the computer showing it: its angle is a straight line in time, θ = θ₀ + 360° (t − t₀)/T. The rotation turns once in 23 h 56 min 4 s [1], the orbit once in 365.256 days [2], the axis once in about 25,800 years [3], the orbit's long axis once in about 111,000 years [2], and the Sun goes round the Galaxy once in about 200 million years, as the apparent drift of Sgr A* shows [4]. Even the fastest hand moves only a quarter of a degree a minute, so the dial looks still; beside it, each hand's angle is written with enough decimals that the last ones change, and a tape graduated in the hand's own angle slides at its true rate. Nothing is sped up.
clock.verdict: Would favour the flat model: ring lasers and satellites finding no rotation of the ground, or star positions showing no yearly parallax.
zoom.title: Powers of ten, from the Earth to Andromeda
zoom.mini: Every frame to scale, the Earth at the centre: the Moon at 1.3 light-seconds, the Sun at 8 light-minutes, the nearest star at 4.2 light-years, the Galactic centre at 27,000, Andromeda at 2.5 million.
zoom.text: The field of view widens tenfold every second and a half, from 20,000 km to four million light-years, the Earth always at the centre. Each object sits at its measured distance from us, in its own direction [1]: the Moon at 384,400 km, the Sun at 149.6 million km, Neptune at 4,500 million km, Proxima Centauri at 4.25 light-years, the Galactic centre at about 27,000 light-years, the Andromeda galaxy at 2.5 million. Each frame has its own scale bar. The empty frames are empty because space is: between the Sun's planets and the nearest star lie four light-years of nothing visible at that scale.
zoom.verdict: Would favour the flat model: a Sun and a Moon a few thousand kilometres away, as triangulation from a plane gives, instead of the distances that laser echoes, light time and Doppler shifts measure.
